title: Clustered integer execution with duplicated integer register files
decision: Split the four integer units into two clusters (U0, U1), each with its own copy of the 80-entry integer register file (4 read / 6 write ports per copy), kept coherent with a 1-cycle cross-cluster write delay.
alternatives_or_rejected: A single unified integer register file with 8 read and 6 write ports — rejected because its physical width would stretch the datapath and exceed the cycle-time target.
rationale: Fewer read/write ports per register file reduce datapath width so the register file does not become the cycle-time limiter; the 1-cycle inter-cluster penalty costs only ~1% performance per simulation.
outcome: 21264 achieves 500–600 MHz cycle time; simulated performance loss from the inter-cluster delay is ~1%, and from static subcluster pre-assignment is 1–2%.
weakest_point: The exact 1% / 1–2% simulation figures and the explicit '8 read / 6 write rejected' wording are corroborated by a contemporary Microprocessor Report article drawn from the same design team; the paper may phrase it differently.

title: Performance leadership via high clock speed + out-of-order, not brainiac-style widening
decision: Pursue performance leadership by combining a uniquely high clock (500–600 MHz at 0.35 µm, six metal layers) with advanced out-of-order and speculative execution, while remaining software-compatible with prior Alpha generations.
rationale: A unique combination of high clock speeds and advanced microarchitectural techniques, including many forms of out-of-order and speculative execution, provide exceptional core computational performance.
outcome: 30+ SPECint95 and 58+ SPECfp95; 50–200% faster than 21164 on many applications while keeping the same 4-instruction fetch width.
weakest_point: Whether the paper frames this as an explicit decision against a 'brainiac' alternative, or simply reports it as the achieved combination.

title: 20-entry integer issue queue bounded by pick-2 arbitration circuit
decision: Size the integer issue queue at 20 entries, arbitrating up to 4 issues per cycle via two pick-2 arbiters (upper and lower subclusters), where each queued instruction may await at most two of the four integer units.
alternatives_or_rejected: A fully general pick-4 arbitration across all four units — not solvable within the target cycle time, so rejected.
rationale: The fundamental circuit loop (grant in cycle N, request in cycle N+1) must close within one cycle; a general pick-4 solution would not meet cycle time, so the design limits each instruction to awaiting at most two units, accepting some throughput degradation versus an ideal scheme.
outcome: Up to 4 integer instructions issued per cycle; simulation used to quantify the performance cost of the pick-2 limitation and asymmetric arbiter.
weakest_point: The 'pick-4 not solvable' phrasing is most explicitly stated in a later physical-technology retrospective citing the 21264 issue logic; the IEEE Micro paper may describe it less bluntly.

title: 64 KB primary I- and D-caches with line/way prediction to hide set-associativity latency
decision: Implement 64 KB 2-way set-associative I-cache and 64 KB D-cache (each 2-way), augmented with a line predictor and a way predictor so that branch-redirect fetch can occur with no fetch bubble.
alternatives_or_rejected: 8 KB primary caches as in 21164 — rejected because their small size caused high miss rates and frequent 6-cycle L2 accesses, hurting performance despite being single-cycle accessible.
rationale: Line and way prediction combines the advantages of set-associative behaviour with the fast access time of a direct-mapped cache, eliminating fetch bubbles and supporting 4-instruction-per-cycle fetch at 500+ MHz.
outcome: 21264 sustains 4 instructions fetched per cycle; cache miss latency to off-chip L2 is 13 cycles, with up to 8 outstanding misses.
weakest_point: The 21164 8 KB comparison and 'rejected' framing comes from a contemporary Microprocessor Report article; the IEEE Micro paper itself may not state the 8 KB alternative as explicitly rejected.
